content: The guidelines will be developed in collaboration with universities, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. Derivative products, such as summaries and compilations of recommendations related to iron supplementation, will be created to provide tailored resources that are practical and beneficial for end-users. Special emphasis will be placed on improving access to these guidelines for stakeholders who face significant or specific barriers to accessing information, as well as for those who play a critical role in implementing the guideline recommendations. This includes policymakers and decision-makers at subnational levels who disseminate the guidelines' content, as well as health workers and educators who contribute to delivering the intervention. The disseminated information will highlight the benefits of iron supplementation for menstruating adult women and adolescent girls, particularly in populations or regions at high risk of anemia and iron deficiency. These guidelines and their content should also be accessible to non-governmental organizations working in coordination with national authorities on nutrition interventions, especially those focused on preventing and controlling anemia in menstruating adult women and adolescent girls. As this is a global guideline, it should be adapted to the specific context of each Member State. Before implementation, public health programs that include iron supplementation for menstruating adult women and adolescent girls should have clearly defined objectives that consider available resources, existing policies, appropriate delivery platforms and suppliers, communication channels, and potential stakeholders. Ideally, iron supplementation should be integrated into broader programs addressing adolescent and reproductive health, including efforts to combat micronutrient deficiencies. The experiences of menstruating adult women and adolescent girls with the intervention should be considered during implementation. Ongoing assessments of the intervention's accessibility and acceptability can inform program design and development, improving adherence to supplementation and better evaluating the program's impact. This is particularly relevant in settings where social norms and determinants create unequal conditions and opportunities for different groups. For example, in some contexts, social perceptions related to ethnicity and race may influence how certain population groups access and utilize the intervention. Supplementation programs for menstruating adult women and adolescent girls must be carefully designed based on locally available evidence and experience. This includes data to inform implementation strategies on procurement and supply-chain issues, optimal distribution channels, behavior-change communication, and specific strategies to identify and reach the most vulnerable women and girls. These considerations are especially important in the absence of a well-functioning healthcare system that can effectively reach this population. Reaching hard-to-access population groups is critical during implementation to address and prevent health inequities. Appropriate surveillance and monitoring systems are essential to provide information on the impact of the disseminated guidelines and their implementation. This includes data on funding adequacy, supply chain effectiveness, and distribution channels. The WHO Essential Medicines List (EML) includes medicines that address priority healthcare needs, selected based on disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and cost-effectiveness. Countries use the WHO EML to develop their own national essential medicines lists, and the quality criteria for vitamins and minerals in the WHO EML align with FAO/WHO standards. A plan for monitoring and evaluation with appropriate indicators, including equity-oriented indicators, is encouraged at all stages of guideline adoption and adaptation globally. The WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, in collaboration with the CDC's International Micronutrient Malnutrition Prevention and Control (IMMPaCt) program and international partners, has developed a generic logic model for micronutrient interventions in public health. This model illustrates the relationships between inputs and expected outcomes, applying micronutrient program evaluation theory. Member States can adjust this model and use it with appropriate indicators to design, implement, monitor, and evaluate the successful scaling-up of nutrition actions in public health programs. The WHO/CDC eCatalogue of indicators for micronutrient programs, based on the logic model, serves as a user-friendly web resource for those involved in monitoring, evaluation, and surveillance of public health programs implementing micronutrient interventions. Indicators for iron supplementation are being developed and will provide a list of potential indicators with standard definitions that can be adapted to local program contexts. The eCatalogue will act as a repository of indicators for monitoring and evaluating micronutrient interventions. While it does not provide guidance for designing or implementing monitoring or evaluation systems, it includes key indicators that may serve as useful references. Since 1991, WHO has hosted the VMNIS micronutrients database to assess the micronutrient status of populations, monitor and evaluate strategies for preventing and controlling micronutrient malnutrition, and track related trends over time. The Evidence and Programme Guidance Unit of the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development manages the VMNIS database through a network of regional and country offices, working closely with national health authorities. At the global level, WHO has developed a web-based Global Targets Tracking Tool to explore scenarios for achieving the 2025 global nutrition targets, including a 50% reduction in anemia among women of reproductive age. This platform also centralizes information on nutrition actions in public health practice worldwide, sharing programmatic details, country adaptations, and lessons learned to demonstrate how guidelines are translated into actions. The Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA) provides valuable information on the implementation of various nutrition policies and interventions. Since its launch in November 2012, GINA's use has steadily increased. An efficient system for routinely collecting relevant data, including health determinants, therapeutic adherence, and program performance measures, is critical to ensuring supplementation programs are effective and sustainable. Monitoring differences across groups in terms of accessibility, availability, acceptability, and intervention quality contributes to designing better public health programs. The creation of monitoring indicators can be informed by approaches to social determinants of health, enabling the identification and addressing of inequities. Collecting and organizing data on implementation is fundamental for appropriate monitoring. This guideline was developed following WHO's evidence-informed guideline-development procedures, as outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development, established in 2009, includes representatives from all WHO departments with an interest in providing scientific nutrition advice. The committee meets twice yearly to guide and oversee the guideline development process. Two additional groups were formed: a guideline development group and an external review group. The guideline development group advises WHO on selecting important outcomes for decision-making and interpreting evidence. It includes experts from various WHO advisory panels and specialists identified through open calls, ensuring a balanced mix of expertise, gender, and regional representation. Efforts were made to include content experts, methodologists, and representatives of potential stakeholders, such as healthcare managers and professionals, as well as ministries of health from Member States. Representatives of commercial organizations were excluded from membership in WHO guideline groups. The final draft guideline was peer-reviewed by three content experts who provided technical feedback. These reviewers were identified through expert panels within and outside WHO. The guideline's scope, evidence appraisal, and decision-making process began with drafting key questions in the PICO (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes) format. These questions were reviewed and modified by the WHO Steering Committee and the guideline development group. A systematic review summarized and appraised the evidence using Cochrane methodology for randomized controlled trials and observational studies. Evidence summaries were prepared using the GRADE approach to assess the overall quality of evidence, considering study design, limitations, consistency, directness, and precision. The draft recommendation was discussed by the WHO Steering Committee and the guideline development group during meetings in 2010 and 2014. Decision-making procedures were established at the start of these meetings, requiring at least two-thirds of the group to be present for discussions. Members voted on the recommendation's direction and strength, documenting their views on the intervention's effects, evidence quality, values, preferences, and costs. If unanimous consensus was not reached, further deliberations and a second round of voting occurred. A two-thirds majority was required for approval if consensus remained elusive. Divergent opinions could be recorded in the guideline, and voting results are retained by WHO for up to five years. Although unanimous consensus was not achieved, over 80% of voting members deemed the recommendation strong. WHO staff and external experts involved in evidence collection and grading were not allowed to participate in voting.
